text.p: These are the leading stories in the Sarajevo press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- It is high time the international community reacts to mafia chauvinism in the divided southern town of Mostar, a newspaper commentary says.

- Former E.U. administrator for Mostar Hans Koschnik, asked to say who can stop expulsions and crimes against human rights in Mostar, says "only Zagreb which decides on all political developments in Mostar".
- February 10 was "D Day" for the destruction of the Moslem-Croat federation by leading political circles in the Croat-held part of Mostar, deputy mayor of Mostar Safet Orucevic says in an interview.

- Sarajevo-based UPI Bank decided to pay shareholders a dividend for the first time. "Bank revenues in 1996 reached 49.3 million Bosnian dinars, more than expected," Mirsad Letic, the bank's manager says.

- Sarajevo canton police promoted new cantonal police force and new Moslem-Croat federation police uniforms in Sarajevo on Wednesday. New federal police uniforms are dark blue with the federation insignia on the sleeve and the name of the canton.
- A train with 540 tonnes of wheat arrived in Sarajevo for the first time since the war broke out in 1992.

- International police monitors' report on Mostar incident is good because it does not have political content but it refers to a concrete event, said Haris Silajdzic, co-chairman of Bosnia's collective cabinet.
- Michael Steiner, deputy to High Represenative to Bosnia says in an interview that their efforts are not aimed against Croat people in Mostar but against criminals and crime.
- Mostar's mayor Ivan Prskalo, a Croat, says the international police report on February 10 incident is incomplete and it does not include all events that happened that day.
